articles.title: Apple to Mac developers: It’s time to let go of Intel
articles.subtitle: Macworld When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
When Apple introduced its M-series chips, it also marked the beginning of the end for software written for Intel Macs. It’s been nearly six years since then, and Apple has let developers know that they can bring Intel Mac development to a close.

In an email to developers, Apple said:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers. By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

When Apple announced macOS 26 Tahoe last year, the company said it would be the last version to support Intel Macs. This new announcement takes another step toward dropping Intel altogether. A new Apple support document adds this vital bit of information:

macOS 27: Final release to support Rosetta — Intel-only apps will no longer run on Mac computers with Apple silicon after this update.

Now it’s up to developers to determine when to stop with Intel code. App designers will need to determine how many of their users still use Intel Macs before they can drop development, which means that some will need to continue to support Intel for a while. If you use an Intel app, reach out to the app developer to find out their plans.

articles.title: Apple’s China AI strategy now includes training its own custom model, per report

articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

china

Apple is reportedly taking a new route to bring artificial intelligence features to customers in China: training a large language model of its own with help from Alibaba.

Reuters reports that three sources described the China-specific model as a departure from Apple’s strategy of relying on third-party models.

Alibaba reportedly supported the model’s training, though neither company commented.

Models including ChatGPT and Claude are unavailable in mainland China, making Apple’s strategy there different from its approach in other major markets for now.

The development follows Alibaba confirming its Apple partnership in February 2025. More recently, China’s internet regulator registered Apple Intelligence for use on iPhones.

Previous reporting said Alibaba’s Qwen model and technology from Baidu would be incorporated into the localized system.

Reuters says it remains unclear how Apple’s new model will work alongside those third-party models. Apple Intelligence is expected to reach China in the coming months following an iOS update, according to the report.

Elsewhere, Apple’s overhauled Siri AI is scheduled to launch publicly with iOS 27 this fall where available.

It will initially support select English variants, while iPhone and iPad availability in the EU is delayed. China’s timeline remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: New PUBG Game Is About ‘Hijinks’ and ‘A Beer With the Boys’
articles.subtitle: Inspired by 'Tarantino and Italian zombie horror' During Gamescom 2026's Opening Night Live showcase, Krafton revealed a brand-new game set in the same universe as PUBG: Dednet. It looked utterly bonkers.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Inspired by 'Tarantino and Italian zombie horror'

During Gamescom 2026's Opening Night Live showcase, Krafton revealed a brand-new game set in the same universe as PUBG: Dednet. It looked utterly bonkers. Set to Ministry’s song “Jesus Built My Hotrod,” it featured a woman getting her face blown off before she could answer a ringing phone, a blazing truck almost running over a player with a light machine gun, three players sliding on their bellies down a grassy slope, another player replacing his arms with machete blades… the list goes on.

The thing is, apart from clearly being a balls-to-the-wall multiplayer FPS, when the trailer concluded, nobody was any the wiser about what it actually was. Is it another battle royale? An arena shooter? An extraction shooter? The following day, I sat down with the game's creative director, Dave Curd, a man who has worked at PUBG Studios for over nine years, to find out exactly what PUBG Dednet is and why we should be excited.

"This is a game about going on a run," he told me (but thankfully not the exercise kind). "A run is a multi-match journey where between each match, you're gathering strange, weird new abilities and mitigating funny injuries to make your dream build and become the king of killers." The reason for this approach? He explained that Dednet will allow the team to offer "pace and persistence," two things that can't be found in the classic PUBG experience.

"What I mean by pace is the animation and gunplay, the movement, the traversal, the frequency of encounters, the minimalization of downtime kind of turned up to 11. And then the persistence totally breaks PUBG's foundation of one game, totally fair, may the best man win." In essence, PUBG Dednet is a multiplayer FPS roguelite. Curd described roguelite mechanics to me as "the ultimate one more spicy chip seasoning that this genre desperately lacks."

Where PUBG might see you go on a losing streak and result in you calling it a night, Curd explains that "every match, win or lose, you're moving your character forward" in Dednet. And he thinks the two can exist in harmony: "When I want something slow, deliberate, tactical, am I the smartest shooter? You're not gonna do better than PUBG. But when it's time to crack open a beer and play with the boys and get into some fucking hijinks? Yeah, Dednet is gonna be your game."

Image: PUBG Studios/Krafton

Those hijinks certainly sound entertaining, too. Curd explained that you can turn into a "little baby doll with a drill arm" then hide in a locker, biding your time, or as seen in the trailer, you can chop your own arms off and replace them with machete blades.

And if you combine the latter with the ability to snake through the grass, alongside an ability called "peekaboo" which allows you to see enemy outlines through walls (and vice versa, to stop it from being ridiculously overpowered), that's the most meta build in the team's early playtests.

You become "some asshole on the ground with blades, sliding all over the place," and it sounds like he's both impressed at its ridiculousness and tired of its prevalence.

But that's exactly what Dednet is going for; everything is over the top. Even the way matches begin is wacky. The team has a system called "wake 100," because PUBG Dednet matches start with the player waking up somewhere, and eventually they want 100 of these scenarios… The only problem is, they've only got about five right now, Curd said with a laugh. Examples include waking up in a body bag, being dropped from a helicopter, being in a box at the bottom of a lake, that sort of thing.

He described it as a "tactical infil," though, because these aren't random. You can choose your spawn location, right up until the match starts, and you can also see where everyone else is picking. So you can hot drop by choice, knowing how many players you'll have to contend with right from the get-go. Alternatively, you can go somewhere by yourself and loot up in peace.

Image: PUBG Studios/Krafton

This element is where Dednet sounds very battle royale-adjacent, and makes me wonder why seemingly splitting the PUBG player base is a smart move. This isn't the only PUBG universe game in the works: Black Budget is another FPS that has had some public playtests, but that is an out-and-out extraction shooter, so will bring in a different audience. There was also Blindspot, a tactical shooter that launched in February of this year into Steam Early Access, then shut down after less than two months.

Unlike the studio's other games though, Dednet has a story to it. The bright, bold outfits seen in the trailer aren't just skins, they're unique characters. And while each character can mix-and-match abilities — this isn't a hero shooter — they have their own personal quests and connections to one another, including alliances and rivalries.

articles.title: Apple’s loaded September kicks off with ‘huge launch’ next week
articles.subtitle: Macworld September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more. This year is especially monumental.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
September is always the biggest month of the year for Apple fans. That’s when we get the new operating systems first announced at WWDC in June, new iPhones, new Apple Watches, and sometimes more.

This year is especially monumental. It’s the first month and the first event helmed by new CEO John Ternus, the release of the biggest OS updates in years with an all-new Siri, and the unveiling of Apple’s first folding iPhone. All that and more are coming this September. Here’s what’s on the way.

New CEO, new iPhone, and more

As of September 1, Tim Cook is out as CEO (taking a backseat role as Chairman) and new CEO John Ternus is at the helm. That means the big Apple event on September 9 will be the first not headlined by Cook in 15 years. In his welcome letter to employees, he promised a “huge launch that’s going to be phenomenal.

” With Ternus at the helm, will the Surprise and Shine event be different in tone or structure from what we’ve seen the last few years? We’ll find out on September 9 at 10 am. Here’s what we expect at the event:

iPhone Ultra: The marquee product of the new lineup will be Apple’s first foldable device, likely to be called iPhone Ultra. We already have a good idea of its design, but we don’t yet know about its features, particularly what Apple is doing with the software. We expect the price to top $2,000.

iPhone 18 Pro/Max: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be an evolutionary upgrade from the iPhone 17 Pro. The big updates are a faster A20 Pro processor and a new main camera with variable aperture.

Apple Watch Series 12: We don’t expect much to be new about the Apple Watch Series 12. There should be a faster processor, and Apple is said to be bringing back the ceramic case option, but the rumors say not to expect a change to the design or major new features this year.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: Just like the Series 12, the new Ultra is going to be primarily a “chip and ship” update with no major design changes or new features.

Apple’s iPhone event will be loaded with shiny new products—and hopefully some surprises.

Apple

AirPods 5: Apparently, there’s an AirPods 5 that could ship as early as September. Like AirPods 4, it would come in both standard and active noise-cancelling versions, but we’re not sure what will actually be new. This is not expected to be the AirPods with cameras in them, and it’s unknown what the new features might be.

Apple TV 4K: A new-generation Apple TV box with a new processor that supports the new Siri AI is supposed to ship before the end of the year. It could be announced at the September event, or it could just go up on the website one day. There’s plenty of time for this update to be released in later months, too.

HomePod mini: Just like the new Apple TV box, the main reason for this to exist is to get a new chip that supports Siri AI. As with the Apple TV, this may not even get mentioned at the event at all and could just go up on the website as an update anytime this year.

Smart home hub: The biggest question mark for Apple’s upcoming event is whether or not the company will unveil its new home hub device. This is said to be a tablet-like pad, with a new 7-inch squarish shape, that will come in both base/speaker-mounted or wall-mounted varieties. It will run a new operating system that blends some of the features of Apple Watch and Apple TV.

It’s meant to control your smart home stuff, make FaceTime calls, listen to music, and so on. Rumors say it could launch this fall, but that doesn’t necessarily mean September.

Mac mini and Mac Studio: While announced in August, the new M6 / M5 Pro Mac mini and M5 Max/Ultra Mac Studio are actually shipping starting on September 22.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: 30,000 people line up 24 hours early to play the final Wardogs closed beta, developer responds: 'YOU PEOPLE ARE CRAZY'
articles.subtitle: Wardogs is holding one more closed beta before launch.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
The hottest FPS in town, Wardogs, is holding one last beta before it hits early access from September 3 to 6. Buzz for the 100-player milsim has far eclipsed the expectations of developer Bulkhead, who says Wardogs has surpassed a million wishlists on Steam.

Bulkhead was planning to keep the final beta a surprise drop for its upcoming FPS Games Show livestream, but decided to spill the beans itself after fans got the wrong idea from teasers. The popular theory was that Bulkhead was preparing an open beta that anyone could join, but game director Joe Brammer clarified on X this week that you'll need to pre-order for $40 to get in, and explained why:

"In this situation, what we’re doing is starting a controlled fire and seeing what burns the fastest to help us prevent and manage a blaze if one does occur in the future,' Brammer said. "If we open the flood gates, very very few systems hold up to the numbers we hit in our first beta, having 100,000 players spam a queue, isn’t that useful to us. What we want to know is really boring stuff, like “what happens when over 100k players are in the server browser, and everyone is clicking on servers."

Basically, Bulkhead is treating the beta like a true stress test—"Obliterate our servers," as the latest trailer dares. Going fully open would be a useful test were Wardogs free-to-play, but what they'd rather do is test against the audience size that's likely to show up on the September 10 early access launch.

The second WARDOGS Closed Beta starts soon.September 3rd | 18:00 UTC | @FPSGamesShowShare your best moments, clips or streams, and tag us.Pre-Order to Access:🔗https://t.co/bXo2yiosVM pic.twitter.com/8ivHmmBXAy September 2, 2026

And Bulkhead will have its hands full with closed beta participants, if past tests are any indication. A playtest held a few weeks ago had nearly 500,000 players and crammed servers so hard that nobody could play for the first hour.

Today, Bulkhead enabled the firing range to let players test out guns 24 hours before the beta begins, and tens of thousands of people are showing up to shoot dummies and drive humvees around in circles, to Bulkhead's disbelief.

WHY ARE 25,000 OF YOU GETTING INTO THE SHOOTING RANGE, YOU PEOPLR ARE CRAZY. September 2, 2026

"WHY ARE 25,000 OF YOU GETTING INTO THE SHOOTING RANGE, YOU PEOPLE ARE CRAZY," Brammer posted today.

The firing range would eventually peak at 30,000 today. Wardogs has its issues out of the gate, but its format is unique and fundamentals very strong. People really want back in, and I'm among them.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour.

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

articles.title: Judge Dredd Meets Studio Ghibli in the Most Exciting Cyberpunk Game in Years
articles.subtitle: No Law breaks all the rules Jump Links No Law is reinventing cyberpunk as we know it It’s pretty weird that vents in video games always open into immaculate stainless steel tunnels. That’s not the case in No Law.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
No Law breaks all the rules

Jump Links

No Law is reinventing cyberpunk as we know it

It’s pretty weird that vents in video games always open into immaculate stainless steel tunnels. That’s not the case in No Law. The vents in No Law are downright disgusting, full of cockroaches and cobwebs. It’s a subtle design choice, but one of many that makes No Law the most exciting game I previewed at Gamescom 2026.

No Law, an immersive sim from Neon Giant, aims to completely reimagine the cyberpunk genre as we know it, at least based on an hour of hands-off gameplay I was shown behind closed doors at Gamescom 2026. Neon Giant’s previous game, the 2021 isometric co-op shooter The Ascent, featured a pretty nuts-and-bolts cyberpunk setting: a vertical city trapped in eternal night, drenched as much in neon as it is in perpetual downpour. No Law offers a more refreshing twist.

No Law is reinventing cyberpunk as we know it

For starters, No Law lets you see — make sure you’re sitting down — the sun. Yes, sunlight! In a cyberpunk game! Its setting, the fictional city of Port Desire, is what Neon Giant considers a sort of Mediterranean cyberpunk. Your Akira s, Cyberpunk 2077 s, and Ghostrunner s are often set in places that riff on Tokyo or Los Angeles. Why never Old World Europe?

Port Desire’s winding alleys and bustling piazzas could be Menton, Sanremo, or any other jewel of the Riviera, except overlaid with the neon signs and strip club advertisements you’ve come to recognize from the genre.

Image: Neon Giant/Krafton

Port Desire is also an incredibly green city, which gives the whole thing a more “one with nature” vibe than you typically see in cyberpunk media. In the fiction of No Law, the city is overrun by aggressive plantlife. Workers have to spend each night using chemicals to clear the growth, else it’ll take over the city.

You can, apparently, find parts of town that have been completely given over to the plants, though I didn’t see any in my demo. (A representative for the studio described it as “Studio Ghibli meets Judge Dredd. ”)

Neon Giant is so committed to creating a sense of place that it named every single street and put all of those names on dedicated street signs, numbering every single building too. If you’d like, during missions, you can let a waypoint direct you exactly where you need to go.

Or you can try to uncover information (either from files or from NPCs) to learn where you need to go, finding those locations based on your understanding of Port Desire’s road network. Additionally, every single NPC has their own home tied to a specific address, which they return to when, say, no longer on shift or no longer interested in getting hammered in the public square.

That last aspect seems innocuous but is quietly the most exciting part of No Law, teasing the sheer breadth of possible outcomes. You play as a fixer named Grey Harker. Burly. Ex-military. The type of blank-slate tough character who serves as a canvas for “doing whatever you want.

” Now let’s say that means you kill the owner of a local bodega, where you’d typically buy health-restoring sodas, status-inflicting alcohol, or, for the hell of it, eggs. That bodega will summarily be closed for the rest of the game.

Image: Neon Giant/Krafton

But let’s say you, a good person, have no intention of killing said bodega owner. Later on, you go on a mission, and get cornered in a courtyard by some thugs. The bodega owner happens to live in the apartment on the third floor. It’s night time. They’re home. You throw a careless grenade at the thugs, miss, and it sails through the bodega owner’s window. That too would shut down the bodega for the rest of your playthrough — without you even realizing it.

In this, Neon Giant appears to have captured the spirit of golden-age immersive sims like Dishonored and Deus Ex: Human Revolution. The studio created a whole bunch of interactive systems. Then they let the game rip.

The Mac mini received a major update in August 2026, so for most people this is a good time to buy. Apple announced the new M6 and M5 Pro Mac mini on August 25, 2026, with sales beginning September 22. With the next significant update unlikely for some time, there is little reason to wait for newer hardware if you need a compact desktop Mac now.

For most buyers, we recommend the M6 Mac mini. Starting at $899/£899, it is considerably more expensive than the M4 generation, which launched at $599, but it offers improved performance for everyday work, office tasks, coding, photo and video editing, and general creative use. It is particularly appealing if you already own a monitor, keyboard and mouse, or if you’re replacing an older Intel Mac or early Apple silicon model.

The M5 Pro Mac mini is better suited to more demanding users. Its additional CPU and GPU performance, Thunderbolt 5 connectivity, higher memory bandwidth and support for up to 64GB of unified memory make it a stronger choice for professional creative work, development and larger local AI models. However, with prices starting at $1,699/£1,699 and rising quickly with upgrades, most people won’t need to spend that much.

This guide explains whether to buy a Mac mini now, which M6 or M5 Pro model suits different users, what to pay, alternatives, refurbished options, drawbacks, and where to buy.

Should you buy a Mac mini now?

There are reasons to wait. Discounts are likely to improve in the months after launch, particularly around Prime Day in October and Black Friday in November, and more refurbished or discounted M4 models may appear as buyers upgrade. If you’re happy with your current Mac, want to see independent benchmarks first or simply want the lowest possible price, there is no need to rush.

On the other hand, buyers who want a new Mac mini at launch may prefer to pre-order. A global memory shortage contributed to long delivery times and limited availability for the previous generation, and similar supply constraints could affect the new models. The higher cost of memory and other components has also contributed to the Mac mini’s substantial price increase.

articles.title: Double Fine's famous game jam returns with 26 new ideas and a promise to make Brutal Legend 2, if its Kickstarter stretch goal is met
articles.subtitle: The Amnesia Fortnight Kickstarter blew past its goal in just two days, but getting a new Brutal Legend is going to be a whole different pile of money
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
One happy upside to Double Fine's newly-regained independence is the return of Amnesia Fortnight, the semi-regular in-house game jam in which everyone stops what they're doing and spends two weeks pitching and developing prototypes for new games. The 2026 edition of the event—seemingly the first since Microsoft acquired Double Fine in 2019—launched a Kickstarter campaign on August 31, and its $400,000 goal has already been surpassed.

The Amnesia Fortnight crowdfunding campaign serves two purposes. It raises money for Double Fine, which is good, but it also grants power: Just like in a real democracy, people who are willing to spend money will get to sway the process in voting for which of the 26 game pitches actually get made, and the more you spend the more influence you have.

At the $15 tier, for instance, your vote only counts for half, but at $30 you get a full vote—and if you go up to $60, your vote is doubled—a single vote cast counts for two! What a great system.

Voting will close on September 6, following the conclusion of PAX, after which the Amnesia Fortnight game jam actually begins: Over the following two weeks, the top four finalists will be built into playable demos, which will then be put out to the public for final voting.

The Kickstarter ends on September 30, after which the big winner will be revealed, and then polished and unleashed out into the world. If it's especially good, it might even be made into a "real game": Previous Double Fine games including Costume Quest, Iron Brigade, and Stacking, and the Compton's Cook-off level in Psychonauts 2, all began as Amnesia Fortnight prototypes.

There are some very cool pitches up on the Kickstarter—here are a few that caught my eye:

Fermi's Playground: Presented by Oliver Franzke. Enrico Fermi famously asked why, in a galaxy this old and this large, we've never heard from anyone. Fermi's Playground hands you the controls: tweak the laws of nature to shift the odds of habitable worlds, sprinkle in supernovae and meteor impacts, run the simulation, and see what a galaxy full of curious explorers would actually take.

Insolation: Presented by Derek Brand. Insolation is a survival game where you’ll pilot an agile spider-bot across a desolate landscape to find and protect the last few species of plants left on the planet. Traverse like a spider. Cling to surfaces, rappel on cables and swing across gaps while imposing machines patrol the space below.

Lucid Gardening: Presented by Matt Enright. In Lucid Gardening, you cultivate a supernatural garden of mysterious plants and animals.

Virtual Pet Manifesto: Presented by Merita Lundstrom Virtual Pet Manifesto is a social idle game where you and your friends are virtual pets. Take care of each other, hang out, and define your new regime, all from the comfort of your desktop.

Lesbian Sled Death: Presented By: Fiona Gallagher. Join the women's Rocket Sled Derby to impress your girl, in Lesbian Sled Death: a four-player, jet-powered, full-contact racing game, where you don't always win by finishing first. (I won't lie, the title is what first grabbed my attention, but the pitch is compelling.)

There are many more, 26 in total, so you'll want to check out the Kickstarter page if you're interested in throwing your weight behind any of them. Insolation is my pick of the litter—not that I have any great affinity for survival games, but I'm a sucker for 'sad lonely robot at the end of the world' stuff. Gets me every time.

As is the way with Kickstarter, there are also stretch goals—one stretch goal, to be precise: If the campaign earns $100 million, Double Fine will make Brütal Legend 2. "Yes, really." Is it going to happen? No, not really: Never say never and all that, but Shenmue 3 was (and as far as I know still is) the most-funded videogame project in Kickstarter history, and it finished with $6.3 million. So yeah, that's a big mountain to climb.

It's possible that other stretch goals are on the way, but Double Fine said "we'll have to wait and see."

articles.title: Mac Studio Buyer's Guide: M5 Max vs. M5 Ultra
articles.subtitle: Apple last week announced two new Mac Studio models, with one built around the M5 Max chip and one around the all-new M5 Ultra chip, replacing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra models that had been on sale since March 2025.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple last week announced two new Mac Studio models, with one built around the M5 Max chip and one around the all-new M5 Ultra chip, replacing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra models that had been on sale since March 2025.

The gap between the two is unusually wide this time. ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Max starts at $2,499, holding the price Apple set when it raised Mac prices in June, while ‌Mac Studio‌ with M5 Ultra starts at $5,499, a further $200 increase on the post-June M3 Ultra price and $1,500 above what the M3 Ultra cost at launch.

That makes the premium $3,000 before any configure-to-order options, and memory and storage upgrades are more expensive than usual because of the memory chip shortage. Our guide helps to answer the question of how to decide which of these two ‌Mac Studio‌ models is best for you. The shared features include:

An identical enclosure measuring 3.7 inches tall and 7.7 inches wide

Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing

Hardware-accelerated H.264, HEVC, ProRes, and ProRes RAW, plus AV1 decode

A next-generation SSD architecture that Apple says is up to twice as fast as before

Thunderbolt 5 with up to 120Gb/s of bandwidth, and clustering of multiple systems using RDMA (remote direct memory access)

10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot (UHS-II)

Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via the N1 chip, both new to the ‌Mac Studio‌

Genlock over USB-C for synchronization with professional camera capture

A 3.5mm headphone jack with support for high-impedance headphones

macOS 27, Apple Intelligence, and Siri AI

Here is everything that differs between the two models:

For the overwhelming majority of buyers, including most professionals, the M5 Max is the more appropriate choice. An 18-core CPU, up to 40 GPU cores with Neural Accelerators, up to 128GB of unified memory, and up to 614GB/s of bandwidth cover workflows such as multi-stream 4K and 6K editing, large Logic sessions with real-time plugins, compiling substantial codebases, and most 3D and motion work.

Apple's own figures support this, with up to 3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio and 1.4x faster scene rendering in Maxon Redshift compared to M4 Max, and graphics that are up to 50% faster than the previous generation. Since memory cannot be added later, the sensible approach is to spend more on unified memory at the point of purchase rather than on the higher chip tier.

You should only choose the M5 Ultra if you anticipate running into a performance ceiling the M5 Max cannot clear. The most obvious use-case is local AI inference, where the whole model needs to be resident in memory. 256GB and 512GB configurations paired with 1.2TB/s of bandwidth allow models with hundreds of billions of parameters to run on the machine itself, which keeps sensitive material on-device and eliminates the recurring cost of paying for cloud inference.

The other workflows that can take advantage of the M5 Ultra include studios finishing 8K material from several cameras at once, where the doubled Media Engine and its four encode engines earn their keep, research and simulation work that needs an enormous memory pool, and anyone who specifically needs six Thunderbolt 5 ports or more than five displays.

articles.title: Perplexity Introduces ‘Hybrid Compute’ for Computer Agent on Apple Silicon Macs
articles.subtitle: Source: Perplexity. Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Perplexity has announced hybrid compute for Personal Computer on Apple silicon Macs. Personal Computer already combined cloud-based Computer tasks with access to local files and apps, but its AI processing was primarily cloud-based. Recently, Perplexity also introduced Portable Computer, a local-first version of Computer that can escalate work to the cloud with a user’s permission.

Hybrid compute approaches the problem from a different direction. Tasks start in the cloud but if a new local classifier detects potentially sensitive information, the user is alerted and asked whether they want to route it to a local model, although users also have the option to let the flagged data be used by a frontier cloud-based model. Gemma E4B, Qwen3.6 35B-A3B, and a Perplexity post-trained version of Qwen3.6 35B are available at launch for that local work, with more models to come in the future.

Tasks that don’t require sensitive information are handled in the cloud by frontier models that also orchestrate the cloud and local tasks. Users select the cloud orchestrator and Perplexity chooses the helper frontier models used.

Another key feature is that hybrid compute works with tasks begun from an iPhone or iPad, too. Those devices could already kick off a session, but now they can also run tasks that use sensitive information locally if your Mac is turned on and running Perplexity.

Yesterday, I got a demo of the feature that walked through three scenarios:

an attorney researching a legal brief, with sensitive client data on their Mac, allowing them to update it locally,

an analyst using web-based data to update a confidential slide deck for a presentation about a company’s financials, and

a small business owner kicking off pricing research from her iPhone that was combined with private pricing data for her business that never left her Mac.

I haven’t tried hybrid compute myself yet, but if it works as advertised, it’s a big step forward for Perplexity, and one that a lot of its competitors are also chasing. AI agents are only as good as the tools and data to which they have access.

Tool calling has been a big focus over the last year and more, but data privacy is an equally important issue that needs to be solved before more companies, especially those in regulated industries, adopt agentic tools like Personal Computer. It’s good to see Perplexity tackling this head-on.

articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: Godzilla Director Reveals the Secret MonsterVerse Easter Egg In His New Action Thriller
articles.subtitle: Tarantino, Godzilla, evil Nazi scientists, and more I’m pretty sure Adam Wingard built a time machine, traveled to the 1970s, and stole Onslaught from some grimy grindhouse movie studio on the outskirts of Los Angeles.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Tarantino, Godzilla, evil Nazi scientists, and more

I’m pretty sure Adam Wingard built a time machine, traveled to the 1970s, and stole Onslaught from some grimy grindhouse movie studio on the outskirts of Los Angeles. That’s the only way to explain how the director behind indie horror hits You’re Next and The Guest, along with Hollywood’s last two Godzilla movies, emerged from the MonsterVerse to deliver the nastiest sci-fi horror movie of 2026.

Onslaught, which tells the the story of a single mom played by Adria Arjona who has to fight off a trio of zombified super-soldiers unleashed on her trailer park by an evil Nazi scientist, feels more at home on your shelf next to Switchblade Sisters and Ilsa, She Wolf of the SS then as part of A24’s summer slate. And I mean that in the most complimentary way possible.

The other, more likely explanation is that Wingard has been studying the grindhouse masters and the auteur directors who swam in their murky, mucky wake for a very long time. Onslaught is his tribute to those movies, and his attempt to update the genre for a modern audience.

“That's the origin of all this,” Wingard confirms in an interview with Polygon. “We're trying to create something that satisfies in a B movie way, but we're doing it with this modern A24 sheen.”

Ahead of Onslaught ’s release, I sat down with Wingard to talk about how directors like Quentin Tarantino and John Carpenter influenced his film, what he learned from making blockbuster Godzilla movies that he brought to this $25 million production, and why he thinks America has been doomed since 1945 (more on that in a minute). Check out five highlights from our conversation below.

Minor spoilers ahead for Onslaught.

1 How Quentin Tarantino inspired Onslaught

It probably doesn't come as a surprise that Wingard is a big fan of Quentin Tarantino's movies. He credits Pulp Fiction with inspiring him to become a director, but says his favorite is Once Upon a Time in Hollywood: "It's the ultimate Tarantino movie."

Wingard brought those influences into Onslaught in many ways. He even brightened up the fake blood to resemble the cartoonishly vibrant red fluid in Kill Bill. However, the biggest inspiration is likely Tarantino's iconic soundtracks.

"Ever since I saw Pulp Fiction in the '90s, that opened a complete doorway to what I consider exciting about creating a directing style," Wingard says. "All my movies, especially the best ones that I think I've directed, all start with a musical approach. That all starts with Tarantino. I love the way he uses needle drops. For the most part, he's introducing you to songs.

He's not just using cool songs that fit that we all know. He's not trying to be populist. In every movie, he's introducing me to things I've never heard. So that's how I try to approach things. "

Image: A24

Until Onslaught, the movie soundtrack Wingard was most proud of was The Guest. "It's kind of hard to beat how many songs I really love are in that movie," he says. "The only one we couldn't get was a Gesaffelstein track."

However, with Onslaught he found a way to top himself by having the movie's Nazi scientist, Dr. Hans Kammler (Dan Stevens), listen to German covers of popular songs.

"There ain't going to be another movie this year that's going to be taking that approach," Wingard says. "There's not going to be an accidental overlap of, 'Oh my God, I can't believe we both used the same KISS song!'"

2 How the rest of the soundtrack came together

German pop covers aside, Onslaught features a pulsing score by Matthew Pusti that combines John Carpenter-inspired melodies with heavy techno and guitars. For Wingard, this was a partnership that had been in the making for years.

articles.title: Dwarf Fortress co-creator says his life as a millionaire is 'basically like reattaining what my parents could do with regular jobs'
articles.subtitle: Tarn Adams lives in a house now. I bet that's nice.
articles.author: PC Gamer
articles.content:
Back in 2024, Dwarf Fortress surpassed 800,000 copies sold, more than enough to make co-creators Tarn and Zach Adams millionaires. At the time, they seemed to be taking a low-key approach to the whole mo' money thing, so when our intrepid interviewer Joshua Wolens caught up with Tarn at the recently-concluded Gamescom, he asked if, in the two years since then, he'd more fully adjusted to his moneybags lifestyle.

"I guess, a bit, somewhat. I mean, I live in a house now. I have two cats and they love me. That's great," Adams said. But, he added, it wasn't so much a matter of adjusting to something new as just going back to what used to be.

"I know what [having a house] is like because I grew up in one. It's basically like reattaining what my parents could do with regular jobs. It's not much different from that.

"And I don't want to make light of financial security, right? I mean, yeah, that's great, and I wish it for everybody."

It makes me think of Adams' comments in the same interview about enabling a more equitable, better-functioning society in Dwarf Fortress by walling up dwarf nobles and abolishing the dwarf cops: He said there's perhaps a " lesson to be had there." Maybe there's a lesson to be had here, too.

Anyway, lest anyone worry about the impact Adams' growing wealth—Dwarf Fortress moved past one million copies sold in 2025—will have on the game's future, that too is moving ahead pretty much unchanged. "We're back to work," Adams said. "I mean, work is the same."

That work is presumably Dwarf Fortress' first Myth and Magic update, slated to go live later this year, which aims to bring magic to the game. And not just the occasional fireball or invisibility cloak: Adams said in August that the goal is to create "procedural magic systems that go beyond combining spell effects and go straight to the fundamental cosmological makeup of the universe." Sounds very Dwarf Fortress indeed.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: Peak Devs Are Using Their Mountain Of Cash To Publish New Indie Games
articles.subtitle: It seems like Aggro Crab has some walking around money and wants to put it to good use supporting indie games and developers.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
It seems like Aggro Crab has some walking around money and wants to put it to good use supporting indie games and developers. The Another Crab’s Treasure developer is pulling an Outersloth, using the windfall it received from creating Peak, one of the biggest indie hits of last year, to spin up its own publishing arm—err… claw —called Aggro Crab Presents.

Aggro Crab Presents is joining a growing club of indie developers that are taking their success and paying it forward. Outersloth is the publishing companion of Innersloth, the makers of Among Us. After Palworld broke numerous Steam records, PocketPair started its own publishing company. In the last few years, more have followed, including the makers of Phasmophobia, and a YouTuber even got in on the wave when videogamedunkey started BigMode.

This trend of indie studios turning publisher is an attempt to respond to the worsening video game labor crisis, demonstrating a more sustainable way publishers can do business.

The contracts these new publishers issue tend to be kinder to developers than those they might get elsewhere, ensuring they get to keep more of their game’s profits to hopefully prevent the all-too-familiar story of developers getting laid off as soon a game launches.

While they can’t operate on the same scale as an EA or an Activision, the games coming out of these publishing deals are often more unique, focused on the craft and fun of game-making instead of chasing broad appeal.

In the announcement, Aggro Crab Presents wrote that it intends to take a more hands-on approach with the games it signs, becoming part of the development process with one important caveat: “And NO generative AI slop.” It’s already signed its first game too, a precision platformer called Rebounder launching sometime next year.

Man, I remember when I was writing about a neat little game about late-stage capitalism ( with funky tunes ) made by folks with a bitchin’ name like it was just yesterday. They grow up so fast.

articles.title: John Ternus is the perfect CEO for this Apple era
articles.subtitle: Macworld After 15 years at the helm, Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO today. In his stead is John Ternus, an Apple veteran who most recently served as Apple’s head hardware honcho and has been knocking around the hallways in Cupertino for most of his...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
After 15 years at the helm, Tim Cook stepped down as Apple CEO today. In his stead is John Ternus, an Apple veteran who most recently served as Apple’s head hardware honcho and has been knocking around the hallways in Cupertino for most of his adult life. If there’s anyone who knows Apple as well as Cook, it’s Ternus.

What can we expect going forward? Tim Cook was effusive in his praise of Ternus, writing in his final message to employees as CEO, “I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John. Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does and I could not be more excited for his leadership.”

But what will the John Ternus era really look like? Will he be able to correct Apple’s mistakes and put the company on the path to further prosperity? And what will that future look like for you? I’ve gazed into the tea leaves, examined my fair share of entrails and read every palm I can find to see if I can work it all out. Here’s what I reckon we could be in for.

Who is John Ternus?

Until being named as CEO, John Ternus was Apple’s Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering, and he’s overseen the physical products that have made Apple such a success. (Apple announced that Johny Srouji will succeed Ternus as hardware chief.)

He first joined Apple in 2001 as part of the company’s product design team, with a particular focus on the much-loved Cinema Display. He graduated to Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2013 and was then promoted to Senior Vice President of Hardware Engineering in 2021.

As the hardware engineering lead, he at first handled Apple’s AirPods, iPad and Mac hardware divisions. iPhone hardware was added to that roster in 2020, with the Apple Watch being put under his purview in 2022. He also played a leading role in Apple’s transition away from Intel processors and towards Apple silicon, taking to the stage and conducting interviews to promote the new chips.

And since the ouster of John Giannandrea as Apple’s AI chief in 2025, the company’s secret robotics projects have been moved under Ternus’s aegis, too.

John Ternus played an instrumental role in the Apple silicon transition for the Mac.

Apple

At 51, he’s also one of the youngest members of Apple’s senior leadership team and taking ober at almost the exact same age as Tim Cook was when he became CEO in 2011, 15 years ago. That tells you that in making this move, Apple is planning for the long haul. If all goes well for the company, Ternus could be in charge for the next decade and a half, if not more.

The John Ternus era

Tim Cook is many things, but unlike Steve Jobs, he’s never truly been a product person. Ternus is a hardware guy through and through, however, and this could help him fix some of Apple’s most pressing problems, such as its floundering Vision Pro and how it makes its forthcoming augmented reality glasses a rip-roaring success.

On that topic, it’s worth noting that the first role Ternus took on after graduating from university was at Virtual Research Systems, a company focused on making virtual reality headsets and other devices. Could that give him uncommon insight into how Apple can set the beleaguered Vision Pro on the right path?

Maybe, maybe not. Ternus left Virtual Research Systems to join Apple in 2001, and a huge amount has changed in the VR world since then. At the same time, Ternus was at Apple during the entire Vision Pro creation process and would have had a strong role in its development. If he were present in a leadership position during that time, would much change now that he’s set to head up the company?

I wouldn’t rule it out. His nature as a product person could give him the ideas and vision to correct course now that he’s got more power concentrated in his hands. It could also be exactly what’s needed to steer the long-rumored Apple smartglasses to a successful launch.

And there’s an encouraging tidbit from a New York Times profile of Ternus from earlier this year. There, it was noted that around 2018, Apple was thinking of adding a LiDAR Scanner to its iPhones but was concerned that the relatively expensive $40 component would eat into its profits. Ternus proposed that the part could be limited to the Pro models and excluded from the entry-level iPhones.

But crucially, he didn’t do this purely because he was looking out for Apple’s bottom line. According to the Times’ profile, Ternus’s reasoning was that the Pro-level iPhones “tended to be purchased by Apple’s most loyal customers, who would be excited about new technology. Average consumers, on the other hand, probably wouldn’t care.”

articles.title: The Potential of M6 and M5 Ultra for Local AI on macOS
articles.subtitle: Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Earlier today, Apple unveiled the new generation of Mac mini and Mac Studio, featuring the latest entries in the Apple silicon family of chips: the M6, available in the Mac mini, and the M5 Ultra, exclusive to the Mac Studio. You can read more details about the announcement and related specs in John’s overview.

As someone who’s been working with an M3 Ultra Mac Studio (on loan from Apple) with 512 GB of RAM for the past year (plus two separate M4 Mac minis) with a particular focus on local AI models and performance gains enabled by Apple’s MLX framework, I obviously am very interested in these new machines.

To give you some context: my current workspace for my upcoming iOS and iPadOS 27 review, which lives in Notion, is entirely managed by a series of local agents running the latest DeepSeek-V4-Flash via MLX on the Mac Studio, which continuously scan the project for new notes, sources, and research material that is automatically categorized and linked in the chapters that I’m writing.

So, yes, I’m sure I’ll have more thoughts on the new Mac minis and Mac Studios soon. In the meantime, I thought it’d be fun to break down the local AI-related details from Apple.

First, the M6. While it may not be the powerhouse that the M5 Ultra is, it’s an interesting new chip because of its new 2 nm process and dual Neural Engine system:

M6 is built using cutting-edge 2 nm process technology, packing greater transistor density into a smaller die for a major leap in performance and power efficiency. M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

But that’s not all: the new 12-core GPU (which has two more cores than the M4’s old GPU) now features Neural Accelerators in each core for the first time on the Mac mini. The result, according to Apple, is “4x faster AI performance and 2x faster graphics than Mac mini with M4”. If these numbers hold up and scale linearly, a local Mixture-of-Experts model such as Qwen 3.

5-35B-A3B, which would run at ~17 tokens/sec on average on a base M4 Mac mini with 16 GB of RAM, could realistically generate output at over 60 tokens/second with the base model M6 Mac mini.

Based on what we’ve seen so far, the one downside of the M6 Mac mini is that it does not have Thunderbolt 5 ports; those are exclusive to the M5 Pro model, also announced today. As Apple also notes, Thunderbolt 5 allows multiple M5 Pro Mac minis to run local AI models as a single cluster (for example, using something like exo ).

Alas, that won’t be possible with the M6 Mac mini and its Thunderbolt 4 bandwidth bottleneck. Nonetheless, I’d be intrigued to compare the performance of the widely regarded Qwen3. 8-27B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash models on the new M6 Mac mini.

Moving on to the flagship M5 Ultra Mac Studio, let’s start here:

With M5 Ultra, Mac Studio achieves up to 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of M3 Ultra and a staggering 9.8x more than M1 Ultra. Combined with up to 512GB of unified memory and 1.2TB/s of memory bandwidth, 50 percent higher than before, Mac Studio lets users run massive models entirely on device with complete privacy — without counting tokens or worrying about rising cloud costs.

As seen on the Mac Studio’s product page, the 512 GB RAM version of the M5 Ultra Mac Studio will only be available in “late October”. Unlike the M6, the M5 Ultra supports Thunderbolt 5, which will allow customers to run multiple Mac Studios in a cluster with shared memory to distribute inference across machines. And, according to Apple, a cluster of four Mac Studios yields three times the performance of a single Mac Studio.

Speaking from personal experience, I know that my M3 Ultra Mac Studio using oMLX can run DeepSeek-V4-Flash locally with generation averaging 35 tokens/second. Assuming a linear 4x increase, that would put the same model at over 120 tokens/second on an M5 Ultra Mac Studio.

To put things in perspective, that kind of performance would be faster than any AI chatbot website, it’d be faster than many providers who offer a “fast” mode for their models, and it’d only be second to either dedicated NVIDIA PC clusters at home or specialized inference providers such as Cerebras or Groq …which are running in full-blown data centers.

Sure, you would need a computer that is likely going to cost more than $20,000 to make it happen, but it’d still be possible on a single machine that is small, quiet, and that – in theory – any consumer can buy off the shelf.

It’s also interesting to consider the implications of M5 Ultra for running much larger models that would have typically required aggressive quantization to even stay in memory and produce any useful output. For example, Z. ai’s GLM-5.

2 (a 744B MoE model) could run at up to 17 tokens/second on an M3 Ultra Mac Studio with 512 GB of RAM; the same person was even able to get the massive Kimi K3 model to run on a single machine…with decoding performance up to 3 tokens/second.

articles.title: Prime Video's Fallout Officially Returns with New Game Tie-in This Week
articles.subtitle: Fallout's surprising new collab is a rare game-to-TV-to-game adaptation The wasteland is about to get a little more playable.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Fallout's surprising new collab is a rare game-to-TV-to-game adaptation

The wasteland is about to get a little more playable. Stern Pinball has begun teasing what appears to be its next major pinball machine, and the company isn't making fans wait long to find out what it's working on.

Stern released two brief teaser trailers on Tuesday, both pointing toward Fallout, specifically an adaptation of Prime Video's TV series based on the Bethesda Softworks sci-fi franchise. One teaser features a Pip-Boy, while another shows a massive Vault door opening. Both teasers point to Sept. 3, when Stern says it will reveal more about its latest machine.

The teasers don't reveal much else, so there are still plenty of questions about what Stern has planned. It's also worth noting that recent leaks and speculation had already pointed toward Fallout being Stern's next major release, making today's teasers something of a confirmation of what fans had been anticipating.

For now, Stern hasn't revealed pricing, editions, gameplay features, or exactly which version of the Fallout universe the pinball machine will draw from. Whatever it's got planned will be revealed just before PAX West.

The Wasteland is having a moment

The Fallout franchise has never been bigger, thanks in large part to Amazon's hit television adaptation. The show's second season took Lucy MacLean and the Ghoul into the Mojave Wasteland and New Vegas, expanding the live-action version of the franchise while bringing in even more familiar elements from the games.

Season 3 is already in production, with Ella Purnell, Aaron Moten and Walton Goggins returning, alongside new additions including Aaron Paul, Emily Mortimer, Manny Jacinto, and Thomasin McKenzie. Amazon has yet to announce a premiere date. The new season is expected to expand the Fallout universe even further, with Lucy and the Ghoul continuing their journey while the story moves beyond New Vegas and into new territory, including Colorado.

There is plenty happening on the game side, too. Bethesda recently confirmed that Fallout 5 is in preproduction, although it remains a long-term project expected to follow The Elder Scrolls 6. Bethesda also revealed that remasters of Fallout 3 and Fallout: New Vegas are in development, while the studio is working with Obsidian on another new Fallout project.

In other words, Stern's timing couldn't be much better. Fallout is currently sitting at the intersection of games, television and an increasingly large fanbase — and a pinball machine gives Stern plenty of iconic imagery, characters and Wasteland chaos to work with.

We'll find out exactly what Stern has been building on Sept. 3.
