articles.title: Diagnosing sentiment in my typo-reporting workflow
articles.subtitle: This is more of a comment than a question. A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo …
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
A few months ago I added a “Report a Typo” feature to Six Colors. The goal was to give people a simple place to go — sixcolors.com/typo — if they found a mistake on the website. That Google form inserts the information into a Google Sheet, and a script attached to the Google Sheet kicks off a simple automation that sends me a notification in a couple different places.

This works pretty well. I’m using a very simple Google Apps script to fire off a webhook when there’s a new form submission. The webhook is running on Make.com, which we use for a bunch of simple web automations, but that’s an implementation detail. Make.com posts an item in a private Discord channel and also crafts a custom push notification to my phone using Pushover.

However, the moment I turned this feature on, I discovered the problem with asking people to report errors or typos: Some people see any open channel of communication as an open channel for any sort of communication. I immediately started getting more “this is more a comment than a question” items about articles than actual typo submissions. Commentary included personal preferences for writing style, web design, political references (real or imagined), and much more.

I’m going to make an admission: This sort of feedback is maddening. I want to be alerted about mistakes on the site so I can fix them promptly, but I am not interested in receiving push notifications regarding your opinion of the professionalism and appropriateness of my writing style.

Unfortunately, it’s an open form. There’s nothing to be done. Or is there?

This is a challenge that can’t really be solved by looking for a bunch of keywords. You need wholesale sentiment analysis of the entire submission. This is—brace yourself—actually a good use of a large language model.

I solved this problem by using a plug-in within Make.com that lets me get a reply back from a cloud LLM that uses a simple model with an API cost of pennies per use, but you could also just use Shortcuts to build a version of this automation that runs on a Mac (Tahoe or Golden Gate) using Apple’s built-in models. It works just fine in Shortcuts on my Mac, via the Use Model action. (See screenshot above.)

Here’s the prompt I’m currently using:

Your task is binary classification. Input: a user-submitted comment about an article, claiming to report an error. Output: one token only: ALLOW or REJECT. Definition of ALLOW: A concrete, objective, verifiable issue in the article.

This includes: * factual mistakes * spelling, grammar, formatting mistakes * broken or incorrect links * wrong names, dates, numbers * technical inaccuracies * omissions of material consequences of a feature or change (e. g. , failing to mention that a feature deletes stored Wi-Fi passwords) Definition of REJECT: Anything subjective.

This includes: * political disagreement * tone or style complaints * metaphor or comparison preferences * ‘you should have covered X more’ * speculation about motives * emotional reactions or rants * admissions that it’s not actually a mistake Classification rules: 1. If the comment identifies a specific factual, technical, or materially consequential issue in the article, return ALLOW. 2.

If the issue would meaningfully affect reader understanding or use of a product/feature, treat it as an omission and return ALLOW. 3. If the comment is opinion, taste, politics, vibe, personal criticism, or preference, return REJECT. 4. If there is no concrete, verifiable claim about the article being wrong or incomplete, return REJECT. 5. If it’s off-topic or spam, return REJECT. 6.

If it’s a short but simple phrase like “there not their” or “r/sheild/shield”, those are nerdier folks reporting typos and that’s fine, ALLOW. Respond with exactly one of these two tokens: ALLOW or REJECT. No explanation. Submission: [[insert report text here]]

Your task is binary classification.

Input: a user-submitted comment about an article, claiming to report an error.

Output: one token only: ALLOW or REJECT.

Definition of ALLOW: A concrete, objective, verifiable issue in the article. This includes: * factual mistakes * spelling, grammar, formatting mistakes * broken or incorrect links * wrong names, dates, numbers * technical inaccuracies * omissions of material consequences of a feature or change (e.g., failing to mention that a feature deletes stored Wi-Fi passwords)

Definition of REJECT: Anything subjective. This includes: * political disagreement * tone or style complaints * metaphor or comparison preferences * ‘you should have covered X more’ * speculation about motives * emotional reactions or rants * admissions that it’s not actually a mistake

articles.title: Apple Announces New M6 and M5 Pro Mac minis, Along with M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studios
articles.subtitle: Source: Apple. Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Today, Apple announced a new M6 chip that will debut in the Mac mini and an M5 Ultra that is coming to the Mac Studio. The company also announced an M5 Pro Mac mini and an M5 Max Mac Studio. Let’s take a look at the headline specs.

The headline feature of the M6 chip is that it’s Apple’s first 2-nanometer chip. The chip also includes “a larger 12-core CPU complex with the world’s fastest CPU core, a larger 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and up to 170GB/s of unified memory bandwidth.”

Looking more closely at the M6, Apple says it consists of two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores and is 1.2x faster in multithreaded performance than an M5 and up to 2.4x faster than an M1. Apple says the GPU delivers nearly 30% more peak GPU compute for AI than the M5. The M6’s 10% faster memory bandwidth will help with AI tasks, too, but its 32GB memory ceiling will limit which models can run locally.

The M6 mini’s GPU sounds impressive, too, with two more cores, Neural Accelerators for each core, which is a first for the mini. According to Apple, that leads to an up to four-fold increase in AI performance and a 2x graphics bump compared to the M4 mini. The Neural Engine has also been improved.

Apple also introduced an M5 Pro mini. It’s understandable if you find it confusing that the base model Mac mini has a more recent generation chipset than the more expensive model. What matters more than the chip generation is the “Pro” in M5 Pro, which makes it more capable than the M6, which has been designed for entry-level models.

The same sort of asymmetry occurred with the 2025 Mac Studio, which included an M4 Max model alongside the M3 Ultra. A big part of that difference is the M5 Pro mini’s support for 64GB of memory (double the M6 version’s top memory spec) and its 307GB/s of memory bandwidth compared to the M6 model’s 170GB/s memory bandwidth.

As for the M5 Ultra, which debuts in the Mac Studio, it sounds like a beast. According to Apple, the chip uses a next-generation version of its UltraFusion technology, resulting in a quad-die architecture for the first time in an Apple silicon chip. In addition, the M5 Ultra features an “up-to-36-core CPU and up-to-80-core GPU with a massive 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, 50 percent more than M3 Ultra.”

Here’s what Sri Santhanam, Apple’s vice president of Silicon Engineering Group, had to say about the new chips:

Today, we’re debuting the next giant leap in performance and AI compute for Apple silicon with the incredibly advanced M6 and the most powerful M-series chip yet, M5 Ultra. Built using the cutting-edge 2 nm process, M6 combines a new CPU complex, two additional CPU and GPU cores, a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and more unified memory bandwidth to power through workloads with amazing energy efficiency.

And for the ultimate desktop performance and the ability to run massive AI models, M5 Ultra features a massive GPU, now with Neural Accelerators, and more unified memory bandwidth, pushing the boundaries of what a desktop can do.

Apple is fusing two dual-die M5 Max chips to create a single quad-die architecture. Apple says the M5 Ultra is “up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than M3 Ultra”, the fastest Mac previously for sale. The M5 Ultra also supports up to an 80-core GPU with up to 4.5x the peak GPU compute for AI tasks compared to the M3 Ultra and features an upgraded Media Engine, according to Apple.

For those who don’t need the bleeding-edge performance of the M5 Ultra, Apple also introduced what sounds like a very capable M5 Max Mac Studio. The M5 Max version of the computer “features an 18-core CPU, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators built into each core, and up to 128GB of unified memory, accelerating complex pro and AI workloads.”

Macs featuring the new chips won’t be available immediately. You can preorder both online today for delivery on September 22 with the caveat that the M5 Ultra Mac Studio with 512GB of memory won’t be available until later in October.

Prices have risen too. The Mac mini models are both $100 more than the models they replace, while the M5 Ultra Mac Studio’s base configuration has risen $200. However, the M5 Max Mac Studio’s starting price hasn’t changed.

The Mac mini has been a lot of things to a lot of people over the years. From a compact, minimalist desktop system to a headless server, the mini is Apple’s jack-of-all-trades. More recently, demand for the tiny computer has surged as people put them to work for a variety of AI tasks, including running LLMs locally and serving as standalone Hermes and OpenClaw machines.

With memory and storage constraints, it’s no surprise that the base prices of the mini have risen. Despite those challenges, I hope Apple is able to produce enough to meet demand. I’ve loved having an M4 Pro model working away day and night in the background. It’s fast, relatively cool, energy efficient, and easy to run remotely.

If the claims of Apple’s press release hold up under real-world use, I expect the new models will be the same, but faster and more capable, which is especially important for tasks like running models locally.

I’m also looking forward to seeing how the new Mac Studios perform in real world tests. I’ve used an M1 Max Mac Studio for a few years now and it’s been every bit the workhorse computer I need for my day-to-day work. However, it’s beginning to show its age when it comes to AI tasks, coding, and other tasks. It may finally be time for me to upgrade.

articles.title: Siri demos in keynote were a little slow, but that’s good-ish news
articles.subtitle: A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: 7 Years Later, What Remains of Edith Finch Still Has the Most Haunting Quote in Gaming
articles.subtitle: Grief is the thing that shapes the Finch legacy There is something powerful about a video game that can make the player sit back and contemplate life.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Grief is the thing that shapes the Finch legacy

There is something powerful about a video game that can make the player sit back and contemplate life. Having control over the character's actions is different from watching those actions play out in a movie or a television show. And when that game is about grief and the choices that can determine the course of a life, the weight of that control feels just a bit heavier.

Like Firewatch before it, What Remains of Edith Finch is a story-driven first-person experience that will stick with the player long after the credits roll. Its quotes, especially, are not easily forgotten.

What Remains of Edith Finch follows seventeen-year-old Edith Finch as she wanders through her Winchester-style home. As the last surviving member of her family, Edith visits her home for the first time in seven years to uncover her family's past. Behind the many sealed doors in the house are memories, but unearthing those memories feels a bit like pressing on a bruise the player didn't know they had. Grief, the game tells us, is not linear, nor does it always follow a single set of rules.

Throughout the game, Edith tells the story of each doomed family member. As the player wanders through their tomb-like rooms, Edith tells the stories of what she knows about them. Objects in the rooms unlock vignettes, told by the narration of that family member. Time feels frozen in place in these moments, and perhaps that is one of the reasons why the way What Remains of Edith Finch explores grief makes the game resonate so strongly.

Dawn, Edith's mother, wanted to protect Edith from the past, which she does by sealing up the rooms of those passed. But her great-grandmother, Edie, believed that memorials were a way to honor the lives people have lived.

The narrative’s profundity, which helped land it on Polygon's best video game quotes of all time, is another reason why the game continues to resonate seven years on. Edith laments the brevity of life to an unborn son that she will never meet through her own narrative, which fills the spaces between vignettes.

"If we lived forever, maybe we'd have time to understand things," she says.

Death is inevitable, but it also should not be feared

If death is the foundation of the home in this game, then tragedy is the wallpaper. As Edith navigates through the familiar halls of her childhood, she tells the story of the seemingly doomed Finch family. Though the members are long gone, their presence is not, and behind each sealed door is another story fated to end in sorrow. From accidents to illness, the player leads Edith through these rooms via a network of secret passageways, which is one of the main exploration highlights of the game.

If there is one thing that the Finch legacy tells the player, it is that everyone will die, but that the little things that make up a life should not be forgotten or pushed aside.

The sealed rooms represent grief shoved aside; even though each room is left as it was the last time that family member was alive, having no way to access them other than the passageways that connect them is like never allowing that grief to air out. The game treats grief like a force, rather than an experience. That force is what shapes the Finch legacy.

There are also moments in the story where the player’s actions sometimes directly cause a character’s death. Knowing it will happen, the player is powerless to stop it as they must push forward for the narrative. This gameplay feels like it must almost mirror how Edith feels on her journey through her family tree. For Edith, each person in her lineage has a story, and she does not want her story to be sealed away from impassable grief like the others have been over time.

However, the underlying message is that grief should not always be linked to sadness. Life, Edith tells the player, is strange and beautiful. Sad things do not define it. Grief is not something that needs to be fixed, but it also should not be ignored.

"It's a lot to ask, but I don't want you to be sad that I'm gone. I want you to be amazed that any of us ever had a chance to be here at all," Edith says.

A subscription will be required to play Square Enix's hit MMO starting next week

All good things must come to an end. After holding a month-long grace period following Final Fantasy 14 's launch on Nintendo Switch 2, Square Enix is reinstating the subscription requirement for Final Fantasy 14 on the console.

Square Enix announced the end of the free subscription period in a post on the Lodestone blog. As previously revealed, while players usually only need one Final Fantasy 14 subscription to play the MMO, playing the game on Switch 2 will require a second subscription. To mitigate costs, the game on Switch 2 will not require a Nintendo Switch Online subscription, and if you already have a Final Fantasy 14 subscription on other platforms, you'll get 50% off the Switch 2 subscription price.

The end of Final Fantasy 14 's free trial period will go into effect on Monday, Sept. 7 at 11:59 p.m. local time.

How do you get a Final Fantasy 14 subscription on Switch 2?

To make the process even more frustrating, Nintendo Switch 2 subscriptions can't be purchased as usual. Instead, players must purchase FFXIV Coins on the Nintendo eShop that can then be used on the Final Fantasy 14 Mog Station to manage subscription fees. FFXIV Coins can also be used to purchase optional items from the Final Fantasy 14 Online Store. Automatic subscription renewals can be set up on Switch 2 but they will only work if you have enough FFXIV Coins on your account.

Players can get 30 days of free play time by purchasing and registering either the Starter or Complete Edition of Final Fantasy 14. Once that free time runs out, you'll still need to purchase a subscription. There is, however, one way to keep playing for free on Switch 2.

If you have never purchased any version of Final Fantasy 14, you can continue to play on the game's free trial without the need to have a subscription. Despite all the hurdles on Switch 2, Final Fantasy 14 runs surprisingly smoothly on the console. For some, it may even be the best place to play the critically acclaimed MMO.

articles.title: App Report: AI to the rescue! No… really
articles.subtitle: Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Artificial Intelligence takes center stage in a few of the apps enjoying this week’s spotlight — and not the kind of AI that’s going to have you rolling your eyes or organizing a protest march against the nearest data center. No, these are actually useful AI features that take some of the busy work of daily life out of your hands so you can concentrate on other things.

AI or no, we’re always looking for top macOS and iOS apps to feature here. If you’ve got something that fits that description, drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief outline of the whats, whys, and wherefores.

Now on to this week’s selection…

Sortio

The folders on my Mac are a mess, but who has the time to make sure that everything is filed away in its proper place? AI does, according to the makers of Sortio, a macOS utility that promises to do the hard work of organization on your behalf.

Sortio taps into AI to look at file names and metadata to help it figure out where to put each file. You can also opt to let the utility read the file, sending a 4KB excerpt to your AI provider of choice for even more detailed sorting. (Sortio also offers an offline mode that uses Ollama or LM Studio to keep its activity on your Mac.) You can further refine sorting by telling Sortio to organize things by file type, project, date, and whether the file is for work or personal use..

I took Sortio for a spin, having it go through the folder of articles I’ve written but haven’t bothered to organize for myself. Sortio was smart enough to take my submissions to Awful Announcing and separate them into their own folder. Not every search is that precise — a separate sorting session had Sortio tagging an offer letter from an old employer named Purch as a financial document — but there are edit buttons to correct mislabeled and misfiled material.

You can try out Sortio for free, which gives you enough of an allowance to sort through a few thousand files to get a flavor for how the app performs. After that, you’ll need to buy a license, with the $14.99/month Pro license suitable for most individual users. There are team and enterprise options as well, and paying for an annual license lowers your monthly rate.

AskPlay

AI isn’t just for organizing your folders; it can also generate a playlist for you based on specific artists, songs or moods you’re hoping to hear. At least, that’s the idea behind AskPlay, an app that lives in your menu bar and lets you type or speak plain-English instructions on the type of music you want to listen to.

You’re going to need a few things besides AskPlay and its $1.99/month subscription to make the app work. For starters, AskPlay works exclusively with Apple Music, so you’ll also need to subscribe to Apple’s streaming service. In addition, you’ll need to provide an API key from an AI provider, with AskPlay supporting OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter.

Those requirements are likely to limit AskPlay’s appeal to some users, but having tried out the app on my Mac, I am impressed by the results. I told AskPlay I wanted to hear songs written by Stephen Sondheim, and it dutifully produced a playlist not just from cast soundtracks but also numbers by vocalists from their own albums.

That said, there were a few misfires — the playlist included a song from Tick, Tick… Boom! , a Jonathan Larson musical that only refers to Sondheim, as well as a rap song that shares a title with something Sondheim wrote. Other requests like “play upbeat songs from the ’80s” proved more successful.

An AskPlay feature I appreciate was the ability to augment playlists. After generating a playlist of Merle Haggard songs, I had the app add Johnny Cash music to the queue. Then I told AskPlay to “add more songs like these,” which brought Waylon Jennings, George Jones, and more to the party.

AskPlay seems built for a very specific kind of user, but if you like thematic playlists and already subscribe to the services that make this app tick, it brings another dimension to your listening experience. In addition to working on the Mac, AskPlay is available for a range of Apple devices including the iPhone, iPad and Vision Pro.

Pocket Screen

I don’t know about you, but my workflow often requires me to jump from one window to another to perform a task — and that can often break up my workflow. I’m thinking of when I’m writing something and need to refer to notes I’ve taken in another application or a PDF I have loaded up in Preview. Jumping between apps takes me out of the flow of writing, not to mention that accurately transcribing what’s in one app to the other can occasionally be a hit-or-miss proposition.

Pocket Screen addresses some of that dilemma by creating a floating window of one app that you can keep in view when you’re working on something else. Think of Pocket Screen as a picture-in-picture feature, but for productivity. You can capture a PDF, webpage, video, chat or other kind of information and keep it close at hand in a resizable window that you can move around your desktop. The app supports up to two simultaneous views, according to its developer.

ChatGPT for Mac now includes an Apple Messages plugin

The optional Messages plugin is not like the sketchy server-related hacks that try to bring iMessage functionality to Android. It’s simply using files on your Mac with your permission when prompted.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Some legends don't need a part two

Double Fine’s new $400K Kickstarter has a stretch goal that reads like either a dare or a joke, I can’t decide which: Raise $100 million for the studio’s upcoming Amnesia Fortnight game jam, and the studio will make Brütal Legend 2.

That’s fabulous, we love to see new games being made, a crowdsourced upwelling of affection for a rad IP will always get me, and I get the dopamine of seeing a progress bar creep to the right, but I think this distracts from the bigger picture: Since the perfect Brütal Legend game already exists, do we need a sequel? Do we really want a sequel?

Or is it time to admit that despite any very publicized crowdfunding goals, we’re probably not getting one? Admitting this would free us up to play Double Fine’s best game again, which is the ideal outcome here, because the first and only Brütal Legend was a wild ride.

Brütal Legend, available to play on Windows PC and Xbox Series X, drops Jack Black’s Eddie Riggs into a fantasy world built entirely from ‘80s metal album covers. Think: amps carved directly into mountainsides, forests where tires replace leaves, gigantic swords driven directly into the earth like obelisks.

It’s an open world that Tim Schafer, the founder and creative director of Double Fine, estimated as covering roughly 64 in-game square miles. Eddie fights battles with an axe called the Separator and a flying V guitar named Clementine, along with spells like “Anvil of Burden” and “Bring it On Home” and “Face Melter.

” It’s School of Rock meets the now-defunct Rock’n’Roller Coaster Starring Aerosmith meets every odd KISS collab meets, uh, 2000 real-time strategy and exceedingly rules-heavy game Sacrifice.

It’s the oddest possible concept, but it worked because it was unique, because it was a tribute to metal, and because — likely due to that sense of “what in the world are we building here” — it got such loving attention to detail. Every faction in the game, from Eddie’s Ironheade to villain Doviculus’s Tainted Coil, got its own aesthetic and sound identity down to the unit design.

Judas Priest guitarist Glenn Tipton even recorded the real guitar solos used for Ironheade’s in-game riffs, while bandmate K. K. Downing recorded solos for the enemy factions, Drowning Doom and Tainted Coil.

If we got a Brütal Legend sequel, what are the odds we’d get the absolute slam dunk of a cast we got with the first? In Brütal Legend, Ozzy Osbourne voices the Guardian of Metal. Lemmy Kilmister plays the Kill Master. Rob Halford voices General Lionwhyte. And Tim Curry plays Doviculus, Emperor of the Tainted Coil, whose ear-piercing screams and squeals will be near-impossible to outshriek in a sequel.

The game’s soundtrack, which is worth it on its own merit, runs from Motörhead to Dimmu Borgir to Judas Priest, and it pairs so nicely with story beats: Slight spoilery teaser, but a castle may collapse to the tune of “Through the Fire and the Flames,” and the final battle is set to “Painkiller.

” This is the game playlist and beat-for-beat storyboarding of a team that loved the music and wanted you to feel the adrenaline they felt as they swung for this risky concept. I would love to be proven wrong, but it feels like a lightning-in-a-bottle situation that would only be tarnished by a sequel that couldn’t possibly go as hard.

Double Fine has a portfolio of very charming games, but none have the same out-there vibe or commitment to the bit. Psychonauts (a 2005 platformer) is beloved, and for good reason, but it lives inside a smaller, safer container: one summer camp, one kid’s head at a time.

Costume Quest (a 2010 Halloween monster-fighting game) and Stacking (a 2011 nesting-doll puzzle game) are charming and modest by design, since they came from quick game jams. Even Psychonauts 2, one of the studio’s most polished releases and a lovely game in its own right, feels cautious: It’s a known formula, executed well, but sans any sense of risk.

If, perhaps, one of the most metal things about Brütal Legend was the fact that it could totally have flopped and the devs went for it anyway — which, incidentally, it did fail commercially — that’s certainly not something we’re recreating in a sequel. Especially if the only way we get a sequel is with a gigantic before-the-fact crowdsourced budget (read: safety net). That doesn’t feel very rock and roll.

articles.title: Apple has released an update to XProtect for all macOS
articles.subtitle: Apple has overnight released its regular weekly update to XProtect, bringing it to version 5358, for all versions […]
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
Apple has overnight released its regular weekly update to XProtect, bringing it to version 5358, for all versions of macOS. As usual it doesn’t release information about what security issues this update might address.

This version adds six new Yara rules for the longstanding Dubrobber family and the recent ShadyShoelace, in MACOS.DUBROBBER.SAINDY, MACOS.DUBROBBER.CHREIM, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.OSLOSTA, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.OSLODL, MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.LODLSYDEAR and MACOS.SHADYSHOELACE.LODLSYDEX8. In the Osascript rules in XPScripts.yr it adds two new rules for MACOS.ANGRYORB.JXPL and MACOS.OSASCRIPT.DUEXKE, amends the rule for MACOS.OSASCRIPT.SYPR again, and removes the rule for MACOS.OSASCRIPT.ANMA.

You can check whether this update has been installed by opening System Information via About This Mac, and selecting the Installations item under Software.

A full listing of security data file versions is given by SilentKnight and SystHist for El Capitan to Golden Gate available from their product page. If your Mac hasn’t yet installed this update, you can force it using SilentKnight or at the command line.

If you want to install this as a named update in SilentKnight, its label is XProtectPlistConfigData_10_15-5358

This update has already been released for Sequoia and later via iCloud. If you want to check it manually, use the Terminal command sudo xprotect check then enter your admin password (this still results in an error in macOS 27, though). If that returns version 5358 but your Mac still reports an older version is installed, you should be able to force the update using sudo xprotect update which should work fine for Golden Gate as well.

articles.title: Apple just ended support for three more Intel Macs
articles.subtitle: Macworld Today is all about the switch from one Apple CEO to another, but the company hasn’t yet completed another transition: from Intel to in-house processors in the Mac.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Today is all about the switch from one Apple CEO to another, but the company hasn’t yet completed another transition: from Intel to in-house processors in the Mac. While Apple stopped selling Intel-based Macs as long ago as 2023, several models are still eligible for hardware support… although that number just shrank further.

As spotted by MacRumors, two 13-inch MacBook Pro models from 2017 and 2018, respectively, moved from the vintage to the obsolete list yesterday, and were joined there by the 2018 Retina MacBook Air. This isn’t just a question of wording. Owners of vintage products (generally those which were discontinued five to seven years ago) can continue to get those products repaired, subject to parts availability, but obsolete items (discontinued more than seven years ago) get almost no hardware support.

The only exception is the option for a battery-only repair which is available up to 10 years after a product goes off sale. But this only applies to laptops and, again, is subject to parts availability.

Every Intel-based MacBook is now either vintage or obsolete. (The last Intel Air was declared vintage in January.) But a few Intel-based Mac desktops haven’t gotten to that stage yet. The final Intel Mac mini and Mac Pro both persevered until 2023, and are still eligible for full hardware support.

articles.title: Meta AI is now available as a more capable desktop app for Mac
articles.subtitle: Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI. Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
Meta continues to get serious about its AI technology. The latest sign? A dedicated Mac app for Meta AI.

Meta joins a crowded field of AI apps for the Mac

The new Meta AI desktop app is version 1.0 beta at launch and weighs just 16MB once installed.

Based on initial inspection, it runs natively on Apple silicon Macs with macOS 15 or later, using an AppKit and SwiftUI shell with WebKit for richer chat content. In other words, this is not an Electron app or a repackaged iPad release.

It includes Mac-specific hooks, making the desktop experience more robust than the Meta AI mobile app.

Quick Invoke uses Option-Space to place a compact Meta AI composer over whatever you are doing. A separate dictation feature lets you hold a shortcut, speak, and have the resulting words typed into any app, from Mail and documents to code editors.

Meta AI can also attach another Mac window to a conversation. With Screen Recording and Accessibility permission, the app reads the window’s visible text and captures a screenshot for the next question. This is context gathering rather than computer control for now.

Beyond chat, the sidebar includes Media, Artifacts, scheduled tasks, conversation history, and an “About Me” personalization section.

Users can switch among thinking modes, attach files, generate media, and create recurring briefings or reminders. The app also includes the ability to hide the Dock icon, allowing it to be invoked with a keyboard shortcut instead.

Meta’s recent AI push

The Mac app is the latest in a steady run of releases. In April, Meta replaced Llama with Muse Spark. A May update then expanded Meta AI with more natural voice conversations and live camera-based assistance.

July brought Muse-powered image generation to Meta AI, WhatsApp, and Instagram, although Meta quickly removed one feature that generated images from public Instagram posts. Meta AI also moved into Threads DMs for private chats.

Most recently, Meta launched Muse Code, a terminal-based AI coding agent for macOS and Linux.
